articles.title: Comcast is turning your WiFi router into a basic home security system, for free
articles.text:
First look: Comcast has begun rolling out WiFi Motion, a feature that allows compatible Xfinity routers to detect movement inside a home without the need for cameras or separate motion sensors. The move gives Comcast a way to add a basic layer of home monitoring through software while illustrating how broadband equipment could play a larger role in connected-home security.
The feature is available through an update to the Xfinity Internet app and works with XB7 gateways and newer models. It is part of the company's new Xfinity Shield service and comes at no additional cost.
WiFi Motion detects changes in the wireless signals traveling between an Xfinity gateway and connected devices. When someone moves through the home, those changes can indicate activity. Customers can choose to receive notifications through the app.
The system can be set to Home Watch, Away Watch, or Dark Watch, the latter of which is intended for overnight use. Customers can also turn the feature on or off through the app.
Comcast says it has spent several years improving the system's accuracy. Early versions of Wi-Fi sensing often struggled to distinguish actual movement from normal fluctuations in a home's wireless environment.
"We have spent the last three years advancing the algorithms for WiFi Motion and tightening up some of the irregularities that came with the early versions of Wi-Fi sensing," Kohposh Kuda, SVP of consumer products at Xfinity, told The Verge.
"We're at a point where we feel confident in the WiFi Motion capability that customers can use this for motion detection in their home and for a basic level of security."
The technology is not intended to replace a conventional security system. It can detect movement, but it cannot provide video footage or identify exactly who is in a room. Comcast continues to sell cameras and physical sensors through Xfinity Shield Select, a $15-per-month package that includes an indoor camera, a door and window sensor, cloud video storage, and a 24/7 urgent-response service.
"But for the average household ... this provides an adequate level of security protection," Kuda says.
The appeal is largely practical. WiFi Motion uses equipment already in a customer's home, so there is no new device to buy, install, or charge. For Comcast, that makes Wi-Fi sensing a software feature that can be distributed across millions of existing gateways.
Other companies have pursued similar ideas. Linksys introduced a Wi-Fi sensing service in 2021 but later discontinued it. Wiz added Wi-Fi sensing capabilities to its smart bulbs in 2023. Philips Hue has also introduced motion-aware technology that uses Zigbee radio signals.
Comcast sees WiFi Motion as a starting point rather than a finished product category. The company says the same type of sensing could eventually support applications beyond basic home monitoring, including services designed to help people age in place.
"We believe this is the foundation for what we think we can do with more advanced use cases," Kuda says.

articles.title: FCC abolishes gigabit speed goal, suggesting it is unfair to slower technologies
articles.text:
The Federal Communications Commission last week eliminated the gigabit speed goal established during the Biden administration and declared that current levels of broadband deployment in the US are acceptable. Though fiber networks have routinely offered such speeds for years, the FCC said the gigabit speed goal is not “technologically neutral,” suggesting that it isn’t fair to other, slower technologies.
In 2024, the FCC raised its broadband benchmark to 100Mbps downstream and 20Mbps upstream, setting the new standard by which to judge whether deployment is reasonable and timely. The FCC at the time also set a long-term speed goal of 1Gbps download speeds paired with 500Mbps upload speeds, saying it would use the goal “as a guidepost for evaluating our efforts to encourage deployment.”
Republican Brendan Carr, who is now the FCC chairman, never liked that long-term goal. He proposed abolishing it last year, and the change was finalized on August 14 in the FCC’s latest broadband deployment report. The reports are mandated by Section 706 of the Telecommunications Act.
“As part of our return to following the plain language of Section 706, we adopt our proposal from the Notice [of Inquiry] to abolish without replacement the long-term goal of 1,000/500 Mbps established in the 2024 Report,” the order said. “A long-term goal is not mentioned in Section 706 and could appear to violate our obligation to conduct our analysis in a technologically neutral manner. At present, it is impossible to predict long-term technological developments and the evolution of consumer preferences.”
The FCC said that comments submitted by cable industry group NCTA and wireless industry group CTIA “support our reasoning for abolishing the long-term goal.”
Gigabit goal “prejudicial” to satellite and wireless
The Carr FCC said last year that the gigabit goal “may be unreasonably prejudicial to technologies such as satellite and fixed wireless that presently do not support such speeds.” But in last week’s report, it said it is not eliminating the goal merely to help providers of slower technology.

articles.title: Meshy 3D Agent: 3D-Modelle per Chat erstellen – ohne CAD-Software
articles.text:
KI-Agenten erobern die 3D-Welt – aber das eigentliche Problem ist ein anderes
Erst Code, dann Text, Bilder, Musik: KI-Agenten haben zuletzt eine kreative Disziplin nach der anderen übernommen. 3D galt lange als zu sperrig – zu viel Geometrie, Topologie und Textur für einen einzelnen Prompt. Mit dem Meshy 3D Agent soll auch diese Hürde fallen: Man beschreibt, was man will, und führt ein Gespräch, bis das Modell steht. Das klingt nach dem nächsten Hype – ist aber der falsche Reflex. Denn ein 3D-Objekt zu erzeugen, war selten das Problem. Die eigentliche Frage lautet: Lässt sich das Ergebnis auch benutzen?
Wie 3D bisher entstand
Klassisch entsteht ein 3D-Modell von Hand – in Spezialsoftware wie Blender, Maya oder ZBrush. Das ist ein Handwerk mit langer Lernkurve; wer es nicht beherrscht, vergibt jeden Auftrag nach außen. Die erste Generation von KI-Werkzeugen verkürzte das drastisch: Aus einem Prompt entsteht in Sekunden ein Modell. Doch das blieb meist ein Schuss ins Blaue – ein Prompt, ein Ergebnis, das man danach selbst nachbessert. Genau hier setzt der dialogbasierte Ansatz an.
Warum ein Dialog mehr ist als ein weiterer Generator
Der Meshy 3D Agent dreht dieses Prinzip um: Er schlägt Richtungen vor, erzeugt mehrere Varianten, verfeinert auf Zuruf und behält den Kontext. Statt zu raten, näherst du dich Schritt für Schritt einem nutzbaren Modell. Nach Angaben von Meshy ist es der erste vollständig dialogbasierte, mehrstufige Agent speziell für die 3D-Erstellung. Seit Kurzem steht er allen Nutzerinnen und Nutzern offen, zuvor lief er als Beta für zahlende Accounts.
Ein Praxisbeispiel: ein komplettes Set in einem Chat
Wie das praktisch aussieht, zeigt ein Beispiel aus der Spieleentwicklung. Ausgangspunkt ist ein einziges Referenzbild einer Szene – etwa eine Retro-Arcade-Kulisse mit Gebäuden, tropischen Pflanzen und Fahrzeugen. Im Chat löst der Entwickler die einzelnen Elemente heraus, erzeugt sie nacheinander in 3D und hält sie im selben Stil. Das Ergebnis ist kein zusammengewürfelter Haufen, sondern ein Set, das zusammengehört. Per Export wandern die fertigen Objekte nach Blender, wo die Szene entsteht. Genau das ist der Unterschied zu einem einzelnen Generator: nicht ein hübsches Modell, sondern ein stimmiges Set – in einem Durchgang, ohne zwölf Einzelteile mühsam aufeinander abzustimmen.
Was herauskommt – und in welchem Format
Nach Angaben von Meshy haben bis Juli 2026 mehr als 12 Millionen registrierte Nutzer über 100 Millionen 3D-Modelle auf der Plattform erstellt, die laut SimilarWeb gemessen am Web-Traffic die Nummer eins ihrer Kategorie ist. Das Unternehmen hat soeben eine Series-B-Finanzierungsrunde über 400 Millionen US-Dollar abgeschlossen – bei einer Bewertung von 1,5 Milliarden US-Dollar.
Als Eingabe reicht, was ohnehin da ist: ein Satz, ein Foto, eine Skizze. Ein texturiertes Modell entsteht laut Anbieter in rund einer Minute und lässt sich in acht Formaten exportieren (FBX, OBJ, GLB, USDZ, STL, BLEND, 3MF, DXF) – direkt in Engines wie Unity, Unreal oder Godot, in Blender und Maya. Für den 3D-Druck gibt der Agent wasserdichte STL- und 3MF-Dateien aus und prüft die Druckbarkeit vor dem Slicen; in Meshys eigenen Tests bestehen rund 97 Prozent der figurenartigen Modelle die Slicer-Prüfung in Bambu Studio. Die Übergabe an Slicer wie OrcaSlicer, Cura oder Creality Print erfolgt direkt.
Für Entwickler: Schnittstelle statt Oberfläche
Auch in eigene Workflows lässt sich der Agent einbinden: über eine REST-API, SDKs für Python und Node.js sowie offizielle Skill-Dateien für die Programmierassistenten Cursor und Claude Code. Ein KI-Assistent kann die 3D-Erzeugung damit direkt aufrufen – als Teil der Pipeline, nicht als isolierter Schritt.
Wofür sich das lohnt – und für wen
Der eigentliche Hebel ist nicht das einzelne Modell, sondern wer 3D überhaupt erstellen kann – und das betrifft nicht nur Spielestudios. Im Produktdesign verkürzt sich der Weg von der Skizze zum Prototyp, im Marketing entstehen 3D-Assets ohne eigene Pipeline. Wichtig bleibt: Der Agent nimmt die Fleißarbeit ab, Auswahl und kreatives Urteil bleiben beim Team.
Wo der Agent (noch) an Grenzen stößt
Ehrlich bleibt: Am stärksten ist die KI bei organischen Formen, Figuren und einzelnen Objekten. Bei präzisen geometrischen oder mechanischen Teilen mit engen Toleranzen wird es schwierig – generierte Kanten wirken oft weicher, als es eine Passung verträgt; hier bleibt klassische CAD-Software die bessere Wahl. Sehr feine Strukturen unter einem Millimeter, etwa dünne Antennen, können beim Druck brechen. Exakte Maße liefert er nicht von sich aus – sie müssen im Slicer nachgezogen werden. Und: Neue Modelle erzeugt er, vorhandene texturiert er neu – die Geometrie einer bestehenden 3D-Datei bearbeitet er nicht.
Lohnt sich der Test?
Wer das selbst beurteilen will, testet mit der Art von Objekt, die man wirklich braucht – nicht mit dem Vorzeige-Drachen, sondern dem eigenen Anwendungsfall. Weil die Generierung eine Zufallskomponente hat, lohnt es sich, mehrere Varianten zu erzeugen und die sauberste zu nehmen – und das Ergebnis vor Produktion oder Druck einmal durch Slicer oder Engine laufen zu lassen. Unterm Strich verschiebt der dialogbasierte Ansatz spürbar, was ohne Spezialsoftware möglich ist. Für Teams, die schnell von der Idee zum nutzbaren Modell kommen wollen, ist er einen Test wert. Ausprobieren lässt er sich bei Meshy.

articles.title: OpenAI seeks to one-up Anthropic with new customer privacy protections | TechCrunch
articles.text:
As AI models have become more powerful, the potential for those models to be misused has grown — as has a clamor for safety guardrails that can stop such abuse from happening. AI companies must now walk a delicate tight rope between respecting their enterprise customers’ privacy while also watching usage for possible issues.
Sensing an opportunity to one-up its rival Anthropic, OpenAI just announced a privacy-centric safety approach to monitoring for misuse. The company is previewing a new service to select customers that it calls Private Safety Processing. This is an automated system that watches for potential abuse while simultaneously retaining none of the customer’s data.
This system clearly runs counter to Anthropic’s recently announced data-retention policy. The policy, which has aggravated some customers, enables the AI lab to keep user data (all of their sessions — and the conversations therein) for a period of 30 days, when it comes to “covered models.” Those models include all Mythos-class models and “future models with similar capabilities,” the company says.
This policy, which was announced in July, was designed for the purposes of safety, allowing the lab to sift and analyze potential impropriety. However, it has deeply concerned some enterprises that handle large amounts of sensitive data and don’t want it harbored (or inspected) by the AI lab.
OpenAI — like most other AI companies — already afford customers a relative level of privacy by adhering to a policy known as Zero Data Retention. ZDR uses agents within the OpenAI API to monitor for abuse on a per session basis. In this way, customer data isn’t retained by the company but companies are still able to scan for bad activity without the need for human intervention. It’s worth noting that Anthropic also largely abides by ZDR — except when it comes to “covered models,” like Fable.
OpenAI says that Private Safety Processing is a new technology that widens ZDR’s scope. It describes it as a form of long-horizon safety monitoring that assesses the inputs and outputs of multiple conversations — not just one. Again, the monitoring is conducted by an agent, which, if triggered, catches interactions and analyzes them across sessions for signs of potential misuse.
The new tech helps OpenAI detect malicious use of AI that takes place over multiple sessions, a spokesperson told TechCrunch. A bad actor — hypothetically someone trying to engineer malware for a cyberattack — may spread out their requests to avoid detection. Private Safety Processing can analyze those multiple conversations for signs of abuse without human review of a user’s conversations.
In the case where the system is triggered, it may send a “narrowly defined signal” to OpenAI that warns of a specific type of activity, the company says. Based on that signal, OpenAI can then decide whether “enforcement is necessary,” it says. If so, OpenAI will reach out to the customer for more context or to work with them on the issue and a customer may choose to share data with OpenAI at their discretion, the spokesperson said.
By contrast, Anthropic notes that human review of customer data can occur, but only “through a controlled access path” that involves “a small set of approved reviewers.” Every one of those review sessions is “recorded in a tamper-proof log that reviewers cannot suppress or modify,” the company says.
The corporate competition between OpenAI and Anthropic is tense at the moment, with both companies looking for any opportunity to gain an advantage on the other. A recent report showed that OpenAI’s Q2 grew more slowly than Anthropic. Anthropic’s annualized revenue run rate is now reportedly $65 billion. Anthropic investors have said it could IPO at $2 trillion, while OpenAI is also working on its IPO.

articles.title: Thunder Compute raises $13M to squeeze more work out of idle GPUs - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Thunder Compute raises $13M to squeeze more work out of idle GPUs
Thunder Compute today announced it has raised $13 million in early funding to help graphics processing unit cloud providers squeeze out the last erg of compute capacity that sits idle and wasted at the long end of workload cycles.
Because GPUs are traditionally allocated as bare-metal resources, dedicated to individual workloads, these expensive chips can spend much of their reserved time sitting idle, waiting for work.
In an exclusive interview with SiliconANGLE, co-founder and Chief Executive Carl Peterson said the objective is to build the “VMware for GPUs.” The idea is to virtualize them so the underlying hardware disappears, much like storage or central processing units. Instead of treating individual GPUs like horses hired out by the minute or hour, Thunder Compute puts them into a pool that can do work whenever capacity becomes available.
“The historical precedent here is that every other type of computer hardware is virtualized,” Peterson said. “For GPUs, this isn’t the case.”
According to the CastAI 2026 State of Kubernetes Optimization Report, enterprise GPUs sit idle, averaging around 5% to 20% utilization. This waste leaves a tremendous amount of capacity at the long end, which Thunder Compute says amounts to almost $200 billion left on the table waiting to be used.
Peterson said much of that underutilization comes from how GPUs are reserved: They are allocated continuously to workloads regardless of whether they are actually being used. Thunder’s software separates a workload’s access to a GPU from the specific hardware serving it, allowing the underlying fleet to be scheduled much more efficiently.
Thunder Compute created proprietary software to treat GPUs as network resources, making them accessible to workloads across the data center. This makes them more flexible and efficient, allowing capacity to be allocated much like storage and central processing unit resources, exactly when it is needed. The company sits between the developer and the cloud provider, abstracting away the GPU as a physical chip so it can drop directly into the existing workflow.
Turning GPUs into another invisible layer
“What’s critical here is that the virtualization is invisible to the developer, and really our goal is for them to not care,” Peterson said.
Importantly, Thunder isn’t really selling a developer productivity story. Peterson said the economic benefit goes primarily to the cloud provider or enterprise firm that bought the GPUs in the first place. Developers should barely notice that Thunder is there; they simply ask for a GPU and get one.
The payoff happens behind the scenes: Higher utilization lets operators squeeze more work out of the hardware they already paid for and potentially pass some of those savings back through lower cloud prices.
To date, Thunder Compute has supplied compute to more than 10,000 users on its own cloud of virtualized GPUs. Peterson couldn’t name any customers, but said two enterprises are piloting the software and the company is scaling it out to many more.
Until now, he explained, Thunder has effectively been “selling to ourselves,” running its own cloud service as a testbed for GPU use cases and becoming its own GPU cloud provider before scaling the software outward.
“Until this point, we have effectively been selling this to ourselves and acting as the cloud provider,” Peterson said. “The fastest way to do that was to launch our own cloud.”
Peterson said Thunder has seen customers achieve gains of four times or more, though he cautioned that the company cannot promise that level of improvement for everyone. The gains depend heavily on the workload and existing utilization.
Now that Thunder has the funding under its belt and has been developing the software for four years, Peterson said the company is confident it is ready to scale across huge fleets of GPUs. The Series A marks a shift from proving the technology on its own cloud toward putting it into the hands of cloud providers and enterprises that already operate GPU infrastructure at scale.
“[The cloud] was a logical place to go, but the most benefit is to work with others who already have huge fleets of GPUs,” Peterson said.
The funding will also help Thunder build out the organization needed to support that shift. Peterson said the company plans to hire systems researchers to continue pushing its virtualization technology, engineers to support enterprise GPU deployments and a sales team as it expands its go-to-market effort. Longer-term, Thunder sees its current virtualization layer as the foundation for a broader suite of GPU infrastructure technology, much as VMware expanded from individual virtualization products into a larger platform.

articles.title: Quarkitech shrinks sensor data before it ever leaves the drone
articles.text:
Quarkitech shrinks sensor data before it ever leaves the drone
The Chennai-based company builds compression software that cuts the volume of data a sensor produces at the source, for platforms where bandwidth and power are limited.
A modern sensor produces more data than the platform carrying it can move. A drone with a hyperspectral camera or a satellite with a radar payload generates data faster than its link can transmit and faster than its onboard storage can absorb, and the gap widens every time sensors improve.
The usual answers are unsatisfying. Storing it for later download makes the information late. Discarding most of it risks losing the part that mattered. Compressing it is easy for a photograph, but hard for scientific data, where the fine detail is often the whole point. works on that third option. Founded in January 2025 and based at the IIT Madras Research Park, the company builds software that reduces sensor data at the source, before it is stored, processed or sent anywhere.
Its founders are Rajesh Narayanan, Sanyam Parashar and Shashikant Singh Kunwar, with Vishnu P.K. as a founding member leading the quantum algorithms work. The company describes its wider field as simulation and algorithmic solvers for large-scale optimisation, the kind of problems that come up in finance and scientific computing as well as in sensing.
Mathematics borrowed from physics
The approach comes from an unexpected direction. Sanyam Parashar, the CEO, has said the algorithms draw on the mathematical framework used in quantum many-body physics, the field concerned with describing systems of enormous numbers of interacting particles.
The connection is less strange than it sounds. Physicists working on those systems spent decades developing methods to represent something vast in a compact form without losing what matters, because the full description is computationally impossible. The same mathematics applies to a data stream.
Quarkitech says its algorithms compress sensor data by 10 to 100 times depending on the sensor. In laboratory tests on drone-captured imagery, it reports reducing data volume 26 times while retaining 98% of what it classifies as mission-critical information. That classification is the company's own, and the result comes from a laboratory test. A practical detail matters as much as the compression ratio: the software runs on ordinary processors and graphics chips, not specialised hardware. That means it can go onto computers already flying, rather than needing new hardware built around it.
Two crore, and a grant
In August 2026, the company raised Rs 2 crore in pre-seed funding from Artha Access, a programme of Artha Venture Fund II, and Finvolve. It separately received a Rs 1.5 crore grant from the IITM-CDOT Samgnya Technologies Foundation under the National Quantum Mission, the government programme approved in 2023 covering quantum computing, communication, sensing and materials.
The grant is non-dilutive, and the combined amount is going into building out the core compression library, hiring engineers, and testing the technology outside the laboratory.
That testing is the real work ahead. The company still has to find out whether the results hold up on a moving platform, in heat and vibration, on limited power, with an intermittent connection.
The applications it names span unmanned aircraft, satellite earth observation, surveillance, and radar and LiDAR mapping. In each case, the sensors are producing more data than the system can move.
No customer, contract or revenue figure is public, and the company is nineteen months old. What it has is a laboratory result, a funded runway and a problem that is not going to get smaller.
(This story has been researched and compiled using publicly available information.)

articles.title: La odisea del emprendedor que compró un viejo crucero, gastó un millón de dólares en su restauración y no pudo disfrutarlo
articles.text:
No todos los proyectos de los que sueñan con tener su propio barco llegan a buen puerto. Ya conocíamos la historia de Clyde Stires, que construyó un enorme yate en su casa. El relato de Chris Willson es igual de interesante. A diferencia de Stires, Willson compró un antiguo crucero de origen alemán y gastó una fortuna en restaurarlo. Después de años de esfuerzo, sus planes se desvanecieron rápidamente.
Todo comenzó en 2008, cuando nuestro protagonista estaba navegando por la web y encontró un anuncio fuera de lo común: alguien estaba vendiendo un transatlántico que encontraba amarrado en Decker Island, California. Sin pensarlo demasiado, este emprendedor tecnológico decidió invertir en la embarcación. Tras cerrar la adquisición en 2008, trasladó su nuevo barco al Rio Vista para poder restaurarlo.
Restauración y problemas
Willson ahora tenía un barco con bastante historia. El crucero había sido construido por el astillero Blohm and Voss en 1955. Los pasajeros viajaban de un continente a otro en una embarcación de 72 metros de eslora que tenía 85 camarotes, diferentes salones, espacios gastronómicos y galerías. No solo destacaba en sus viajes transatlánticos, sino que también había aparecido en la película ‘From Russia with Love’ de James Bond.
Como recoge CNN, el hombre bautizó al barco como Aurora después de pasar su primera noche a bordo. "Me desperté con uno de los amaneceres más brillantes que había visto en mi vida", aseguró. Pero no todo en el proyecto era tan perfecto. Willson se vio obligado a trasladar varias veces el barco mientras realizaba las tareas de restauración, aunque tenía claro que quería que su barco estuviera en aguas poco profundas.
Durante más de una década, Willson y varios colaboradores voluntarios hicieron todo tipo de trabajos de manera "artesanal" para mejorar el barco. Las cosas, no obstante, comenzaron a cambiar en 2022. Aurora estaba amarrado en un puerto deportivo californiano llamado Herman & Helen's Marina, cuando algunos lugareños y las autoridades locales empezaron a hacer presión para que el barco fuera trasladado a otro lugar. Temían un hundimiento.
Un viejo dragaminas bautizado como HMCS Chaleur se encontraba en la misma zona desde hace tiempo y un remolcador militar de la década de 1940 se había hundido recientemente generando preocupaciones relacionadas a la contaminación ambiental. Con una orden de desalojo en puerta, Willson evaluó el coste de sacar el barco, pero necesitaba gastar cerca de un millón de dólares en trabajos fluviales para poder completar las tareas.
Se trataba sencillamente de una cantidad de dinero imposible de asumir. Willson había recibido donaciones para continuar con su proyecto, en parte por la popularidad de su canal de YouTube. La única solución aparente fue venderlo por el precio simbólico de 20 dólares a un comprador que nunca se hizo público, con la esperanza de que un nuevo propietario pudiera seguir con el proyecto adelante, pero las cosas no tardaron en truncarse una vez más.
A mediados de 2024, la Delegación del Sheriff del Condado de San Joaquín anunció que el Aurora estaba hundiéndose. "Se ha determinado que el barco tiene un agujero", afirmaron las autoridades. En este sentido, añadieron que también se había registrado un derrame de combustible diésel, lo que obligó la intervención de diferentes agencias para contener el problema.
En diciembre de 2024, el barco fue finalmente remolcado hasta Mare Island, al norte de California. Allí, las grúas desmontaron su estructura de acero pieza a pieza hasta hacerla desaparecer.
Hoy el Aurora ya no existe: lo único que queda es una factura de 8,2 millones de dólares por los costes del desguace y limpieza, de la cual tuvieron que hacer frente las arcas públicas de Stockton. En la actualidad se mantiene la investigación judicial para determinar quién era el auténtico propietario del barco para que asuman el pago y que el ayuntamiento de Stockton pueda recuperar parte del dinero que le costó poner fin al sueño de Wilson.
Una versión de este artículo se publicó en septiembre de 2025.

articles.title: Amazon to bring 30-minute drone delivery to 500 US locations by the end of 2026
articles.text:
Looking ahead: Of the many sci-fi tropes we've seen over the years, few are as close to becoming real as skies full of delivery drones, and Amazon is leading the way. The retail giant has announced that it plans to expand its Prime Air drone delivery service to 500 cities and towns in the United States by the end of 2026, bringing under-30-minute deliveries to tens of millions of people in the country.
Amazon's dream of widespread drone deliveries has taken over a decade of false starts and setbacks, but its vision is starting to be fulfilled. The latest expansion plan would see its current drone delivery footprint increase sixfold.
The announcement notes that Prime Air plans to launch soon in the Chicago, Illinois; Syracuse, New York; Cleveland, Ohio; Atlanta, Georgia; and Boise, Idaho metro areas, with more communities to come later this year.
 – ABC7 News (@abc7newsbayarea) August 19, 2026
It was almost 13 years ago, on December 1, 2013, when Jeff Bezos first revealed plans for Prime Air on 60 Minutes, showing off the prototype drones. Bezos predicted that the service could be operating within four or five years.
As we know, that estimate proved wildly optimistic. The FAA didn't grant Amazon permission to begin testing in US airspace until 2015, and even then, the aircraft had to remain within sight of a pilot and observer.
Amazon received a Part 135 air carrier certificate, allowing it to carry packages beyond an operator's visual line of sight, in 2020 – two years after Bezos' original deadline had passed.
Prime Air also suffered problems within Amazon. Just weeks after receiving the 2020 approval, the company fired dozens of employees as part of a reorganization and began looking at third-party manufacturers to produce some drone components. By 2022, Amazon had tested more than two dozen prototype designs but had yet to make regular deliveries to US customers.
The service finally launched in December 2022, initially delivering a small number of packages in Lockeford, California, and College Station, Texas. By May 2023, Prime Air had completed just 100 deliveries, far short of its target of 10,000 for the year. Amazon closed the Lockeford operation in April 2024 and shifted its attention to a new site in Tolleson, Arizona.
Safety problems continued after the newer MK30 drones entered service. Amazon temporarily halted operations in Arizona and Texas in early 2025 following two test crashes at its facility in Oregon caused by altitude-sensor problems. Later that year, two Prime Air drones crashed into the same construction crane in Arizona, causing extensive damage and a fire. The following month, another MK30 severed an overhead internet cable in Texas, prompting yet another FAA investigation.
Prime Air is also being investigated in the UK after a drone crashed in a garden last month.
Amazon's drones are capable of delivering packages to customers within a 7.5-mile radius of its facilities. Nearly all items weighing 5 pounds or less that fit in a large shoebox can be delivered by air.
Prime Air boss David Carbon said in March that the company will make 1 million drone deliveries this year. He added that Amazon is testing a new delivery mechanism that could allow its drones to carry a wider range of products, including fragile items such as cartons of eggs and other perishables.

articles.title: The floodgates are open after another Chinese company lands a reusable rocket
articles.text:
It has been a little more than a month since China recovered an orbital-class rocket booster for the first time. A second launch operator accomplished a similar feat Tuesday in another sign of China’s growing launch capability.
It took 10 years for a second US launch company, Blue Origin, to propulsively land an orbital-class booster after SpaceX did it with the Falcon 9 rocket in 2015. SpaceX has since added a second reusable rocket to its fleet with Starship and its Super Heavy booster. Perhaps a third American company will join SpaceX and Blue Origin’s club in 2027. Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, Relativity Space, and Firefly Aerospace—working in partnership with Northrop Grumman—are working on reusable rockets that could make their first flights in the next couple of years.
A similar number of launch companies are working on reusable rockets in China. Some of them operate under the auspices of the sprawling state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC). Others are more commercial in nature, driven by capital investment from private industry.
After years of development, these Chinese launch companies made their first attempts to land their new rocket boosters last December. A company named LandSpace was first when it launched the first test flight of its new Zhuque-3 rocket. The rocket successfully reached orbit but missed its landing. Later that month, CASC’s Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology launched a new rocket named the Long March 12A with similar results.
Then, a third rocket, the Long March 10B from another CASC division, became the first to achieve a successful booster recovery July 10. The Long March 10B’s first stage was caught by a net recovery mechanism on an offshore platform in the South China Sea. Now, 40 days later, LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 has flown again, this time on a flight punctuated by a picture-perfect landing of its first-stage booster in northwestern China.
Landing from space
The Zhuque-3, or ZQ-3, rocket lifted off from a commercial launch zone at China’s Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center at 7:35 pm EDT (23:35 UTC) Tuesday, about an hour after sunrise Wednesday at the spaceport in the Gobi Desert. Nine methane-fueled engines powered the 216-foot-tall (66-meter) rocket on a course southeast from Jiuquan, then the rocket’s upper stage took over the task of placing a single satellite into orbit.
The rocket’s first stage, made of stainless steel, soared to the edge of space, then maneuvered toward a prepared landing zone some 240 miles (390 kilometers) downrange, settling to a propulsive touchdown on four extendable landing legs. LandSpace, founded in 2015, declared the mission a total success.
MISSION SUCCESS | ZhuQue-3 Y2 Reusable Launch Vehicle Achieved Full Success in Orbital Insertion and First-Stage Recovery
On August 19, 2026, at 07:35 (UTC+8), the ZhuQue-3 (ZQ-3) Y2 reusable launch vehicle lifted off from the Dongfeng Commercial Space Innovation Pilot Zone.… pic.twitter.com/fshijOxgtc
“This mission marks China’s first-ever successful recovery attempt of the first stage of an orbital-class launch vehicle using landing legs, and China’s first successful booster recovery on land,” LandSpace said in a statement. “It is a pivotal flight test for Zhuque-3 as it transitions from the technological demonstration and verification phase toward the engineering application phase of reusability.”
LandSpace’s engineers made several changes to the rocket after the crash landing of the first Zhuque-3 booster in December. The updates included using just a single engine for the final phase of landing and modifications to the rocket’s heat shield for protection from reentry conditions.
“This mission lays a solid foundation for subsequent stages, including post-recovery inspection and maintenance, reuse flights, and commercial applications,” LandSpace said.
“The first stage underwent high-altitude gliding, followed by ignition for deceleration upon re-entry, aerodynamic glide control, and finally, a landing burn to slow down,” Dai Zheng, head of the Zhuque-3 project at LandSpace, told Chinese state television. “That final braking maneuver was executed beautifully, achieving a soft landing and realizing our original design goal of a ‘one-shot reverse-parking’ maneuver while moving at high speed.
“Our team will immediately begin inspecting the recovered first-stage booster,” Dai said. “We will collect status data and perform maintenance and overhauls. Once that work is complete, we will put the booster back into service for another flight as soon as possible.”
The Zhuque-3’s basic design can place a payload of more than 17,600 pounds (8 metric tons) into low-Earth orbit after accounting for the fuel reserves required for booster recovery. LandSpace eventually plans to debut an upgraded Zhuque-3 carrying more propellant and using more powerful engines, raising its payload capacity to more than 40,000 pounds (18.3 metric tons) in reusable mode or a few tons more with an expendable booster.
The Zhuque-3 builds on LandSpace’s earlier work on a smaller rocket named the Zhuque-2, which became the world’s first methane-fueled launcher to reach orbit in 2023.
The Zhuque-3 booster bears a striking resemblance to SpaceX’s Falcon 9, with grid fins and landing legs. The Falcon 9 uses kerosene fuel, while the Zhuque-3 uses methane.
The Zhuque-3 booster bears a striking resemblance to SpaceX’s Falcon 9, with grid fins and landing legs. The Falcon 9 uses kerosene fuel, while the Zhuque-3 uses methane.
Second mover
China’s rocket companies still have some work to do to demonstrate booster turnaround and reuse. The Long March 10B booster recovered last month is supposed to fly again before the end of the year, according to CASC. LandSpace did not immediately say when it might reuse the Zhuque-3 booster, but the company previously said it plans to fly each booster at least 20 times.
With the benefits of reuse, LandSpace says its medium-lift rocket will be optimized for deploying Chinese satellite mega-constellations, such as those for broadband connectivity. Chinese officials project the country’s two largest constellations, Guowang and Qianfan, will require 700 to 800 rocket launches over the next seven to 10 years.
Several more Chinese rockets with reusable boosters could fly in the next few months. Next in line might be the second flight and landing attempt of the Long March 12A. Others include the Long March 12B backed by the Chinese government, the Pallas-1 from Galactic Energy, the Hyperbola-3 from iSpace, and Space Pioneer’s Tianlong-3, which failed on its first test launch earlier this year. It would not be surprising if one or more of these Chinese rockets launch and land before one of the next crop of American rockets does so.
The US rocket industry has long been dominant in the two most important metrics: number of orbital launches and payload mass to orbit. This is almost entirely thanks to the growth of SpaceX and its pioneering reusable Falcon 9 rocket. For the past few years, Falcon 9s have flown an average of three times per week, usually on fully loaded missions to deliver more capacity to SpaceX’s Starlink Internet network.
But SpaceX is looking to wind down the Falcon 9 rocket soon and could stop offering the workhorse launch vehicle to commercial customers after 2028. The replacement is Starship, a massive rocket with at least five times the payload capacity of the Falcon 9. It is designed for full reuse to support a more rapid launch cadence than the Falcon 9, which has likely already had its busiest year.
Starship remains experimental, with many milestones to go before it can fully replace the Falcon 9. Starship also has a history of delays, so further schedule slips may cause SpaceX to reconsider the retirement of its workhorse. China is working on a Starship-like rocket called the Long March 9, but it won’t fly until sometime after 2030.
The payload envelope for Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket falls in between Falcon 9 and Starship. New Glenn appeared poised for a breakout year after the first reflight of a recovered first-stage booster, but the rocket is now grounded after an explosion on the launch pad in Florida in May.
The other major US launch provider, United Launch Alliance, has no near-term plans for a reusable architecture. Nobody else is close, either.
This all leaves companies like Rocket Lab, Stoke, Relativity, and others with a potential opening in the market for their medium- to heavy-class rockets once Falcon 9 is off the stage.
China, meanwhile, has a bench that is arguably just as deep as the US launch industry. None of China’s space companies—even the colossal state-owned CASC—can come close to matching SpaceX’s rapid-fire launch schedule. Collectively, they only launch about half as often as SpaceX.
But that is with a fleet of entirely expendable rockets. China’s foray into the realm of reusable rockets could change that.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

articles.title: Google Pixel 11 Review: The one to buy if you need an upgrade
articles.text:
The Pros
- Solid hardware
- Capable camera
- Intelligence that's actually helpful
The Cons
- Tensor G6 is better, but not enough
- Battery can't keep up with heavy use
- More expensive
This year, Google is continuing its trend of subtle refinements with its Pixel line. The new Pixel 11 sports a handful of new features and enhancements, but at first glance doesn’t seem that different from its predecessor.
Moreover, the base Pixel model remains in a somewhat awkward spot, squeezed between a more budget-friendly ‘A’ model — currently the Pixel 10a and presumably the 11a that’s likely to come next year — and the more capable Pro models. (Stay tuned for a full review of the Pixel 11 Pro in the coming days!)
But it’s not just an internal squeeze. The Pixel line (and most smartphones coming out this year) also have to contend with ongoing component shortages, such as RAM, thanks to AI companies and other factors.
The result? A base Pixel model that costs a little more than before without doing much to change the formula. For the Pixel fans out there, the Pixel 11 is more of the same great phone you’ve come to know and love, with a few new features and not much else.
What’s actually new
So, what’s actually new this year? Well, there are a few things. Starting with the hardware, there are some external changes including some awesome new colours (I’m a huge fan of the Hibiscus shade pictured in this review) and Google significantly cut down the thickness of the camera bump compared to the Pixel 10. (The Pro models retain their larger camera bump, however.) It’s also a bit lighter than the Pixel 10, which is always welcome.
The only other noticeable external change is the layout of the camera bar, which trades the Pixel 10’s dual-tone metal and glass approach for a uniform black glass, and a new LED flash that looks like HiLight, but isn’t — HiLight is exclusive to the Pro models.

There are some internal hardware changes as well, including a slightly larger battery (4,985mAh to the 10’s 4,970mAh), more storage (the Pixel 11 starts at 256GB instead of 128GB), and the new Tensor G6 chip and Titan M3 security coprocessor.
Camera hardware also remains relatively unchanged, with the Pixel 11 sporting a 48MP main camera with an 85-degree field of view (the Pixel 10 was 82-degree FOV), a 13MP ultrawide camera, and a 10.8MP telephoto camera offering 5x optical zoom. Aside from the slight FOV change, the main sensor is also larger, which should improve performance in low-light scenarios. The Tensor G6 sports an upgraded imaging signal processor (ISP) that should help improve capture speeds, with Google touting 4.5 times faster Night Sight processing.
There are a handful of new software features as well, like Magic Capture and Camera Looks, and a suite of tools aimed at content creators like grid lines optimized for social media and a built-in teleprompter feature. But we’ll get into these in more depth below.
Fly like a G6?
Google touted some major upgrades to the Tensor chip this year, noting that the upgraded CPU offers 25 per cent faster web browsing and 15 per cent quicker app launches. Tensor G6 also features 50 per cent more compute for running local AI like Gemini Nano — Google says it’s up to 3.5 times faster and uses 3.5 times less energy.
In my time with the Pixel 11 so far, it absolutely feels snappy, though I can’t say it’s noticeably faster than the Pixel 10 Pro I was using before. However, one area I did notice improvement was thermals. I find the Pixel 11 doesn’t get as warm as the 10 Pro during intensive tasks like gaming.
I haven’t benchmarked the Pixel 11 yet, mostly because benchmarking tools like Geekbench aren’t available for the device yet, but once they are, I’ll add the results to this review.
Still, Pixel phones have never been benchmark champs and yet typically offer really solid performance in real-world use. During my testing time, I had no noticeable slowdowns or other performance issues.
Unfortunately, the Pixel 11 isn’t much better than its predecessors when it comes to battery life. With my typical usage, including messaging and emailing, streaming music, browsing social media, watching YouTube, and occasionally playing some games, it was able to make it from around 7 a.m. to around 11 p.m. There usually wasn’t enough to stretch into a second day if I forgot to charge overnight, however.
But on heavy-use days, like when I go into the office and use the Pixel 11 for hotspotting, the battery drains much more quickly. Obviously, hotspotting is a more intensive task, but on those days I was hunting for a charger by 4 p.m.
On the whole, I’d say performance is improved compared to the 10 series, but not by significant margins. Anyone coming from an older Pixel phone may appreciate these improvements more.
Capable cameras
Next up, let’s chat cameras. With the Pixel 10, I felt like the base model was able to produce results that were good enough despite having worse camera hardware than the Pro models.
The same holds true with the Pixel 11, which is able to pump out some fantastic shots. The better hardware available on the Pro models can definitely help in more challenging scenarios, like lowlight or zoom shots, but Google’s computational photography is able to squeeze the most even out of lesser sensors.
In head-to-head comparisons, there’s not a ton of difference between the Pixel 11 and Pixel 10 main sensors. Both produce similar results with good colours and details.
Things get a little more interesting with the telephoto camera. At the base bx optical zoom, results are very similar, although I will note the slight differences in colour. The Pixel 11 does a better job bringing out the green hues in the bandshell compared to the Pixel 10, but otherwise quality is about the same.
Google boasted that the Pixel 11 sports 30x ‘Super Res’ zoom, which uses the telephoto camera mixed with other techniques like AI to improve the quality loss from going beyond the optical zoom’s upper limits. Most of the time, I’d recommend that people stick to the optical zoom, or maybe go up to 10x Super Res — beyond that point, things start to fall apart. That said, the Pixel 11 does a pretty good job of keeping the lettering on the bandshell and other details clear with Super Res Zoom. I’d argue it comes pretty close to the 10 Pro’s 30x zoom in terms of overall quality.
One of the other big additions this year is Camera Looks, which offers four “professional-grade film presets” and the option to create your own. This totally rips off Apple’s Photographic Styles feature that launched on the iPhone 16 series. Based on my testing, I don’t notice much difference between the styles. I also found them to be annoying to change on the fly, so I just stuck with the ‘Original’ style for my photos.
Other new camera features include Magic Capture, which offers a combination video and photography mode. Users can switch the camera into Magic Capture mode and tap the shutter button to start a video-like capture. In the background, the Pixel 11 analyzes the frames and automatically pulls out the best shots for you. On paper, it sounds really neat, but I haven’t had enough time using this feature yet to say if it works as well as promised.
There’s also the aforementioned creator suite with storyboarding features, social media grid lines, audio visualizer, and teleprompter features. I’m not really one to make TikToks or other video content, but these features look great for those who are into doing that.
Overall, the Pixel 11 camera carries on the tradition of being pretty good. It’s not the best camera on a phone, but it’s quite capable and should be sufficient for the majority of users. While I appreciate the extra hardware capabilities of the Pro cameras for work purposes, the Pixel 11 makes a fantastic everyday camera.
Other software goodies
Finally, Google added a ton of new software goodies to the Pixel 11, some of which will likely make their way to older Pixels (if they haven’t already). Google’s Magic Cue system got an upgrade and is now called ‘Proactive Assistance.’ I still don’t find it as useful as Google thinks it is, but I’m definitely seeing it more often on the Pixel 11 than I did on the Pixel 10 or 10 Pro. I’ve already used it a few times to add events to my calendar, which is quite handy.
Proactive Assistance can also show up in new ways, such as location-based tips appearing in Pixel’s ‘At a Glance’ widget on the home screen. However, this capability is still in preview, and it hasn’t shown up yet for me.
Elsewhere, Google’s Live Translate got an upgrade that allows for real-time speech-to-speech translation, enabling the phone to automatically dub videos into your language.
And for speech-to-text enthusiasts, the Pixel 11 sports Rambler, which is better able to strip out filler words so you can speak more naturally when using voice input.
While the above changes are all welcome, I’m not sure any of these are compelling enough to drive a phone purchase. They feel more like nice bonuses that make an upgrade you’re already doing feel better, rather than must-have capabilities that will move phones.
Worth the upgrade?
On the whole, the Pixel 11 is a really good phone. It gets a lot right, has a solid camera system, and a bunch of smart features that make the phone feel more helpful than competitors. At the same time, Google’s hardware remains a bit behind the curve, and price increases don’t help matters either.
The Pixel 11 retails for $1,249 for the 256GB model in Canada, or $1,419 for the 512GB. Last year’s Pixel 10, on the other hand, cost $1,099 for the 128GB model and $1,229 for the 256GB. So the price increase isn’t huge if you compare the 256GB options, but the lack of a cheaper 128GB model definitely hurts here.
While it’s generally a bad year to upgrade your tech thanks to all of the rising prices, I do think that those with older Pixel models like the 7 or 8 would see enough benefits to justify an upgrade. And if you’re trying to choose between the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro, I’d say stick with the 11 unless you’re a real camera snob.
For what it’s worth, this is the Pixel phone I would buy for myself if I were in the market for an upgrade.
The Google Pixel 11 is available for pre-order now, and launches on Aug. 20, 2026.

articles.title: Las filtraciones de 'GTA 6' no se detienen y ya son la peor pesadilla de Rockstar
articles.text:
Las filtraciones de GTA 6 sumaron un nuevo episodio en las últimas horas con la aparición de un nuevo vídeo mostrando el gameplay del esperado juego de Rockstar Games. Pero esta no fue una filtración más, pues reveló que los autores de los leaks tendrían en su poder una versión jugable del nuevo Grand Theft Auto.
El más reciente vídeo de GTA 6, el quinto que se ha divulgado en lo que va de esta semana, incluye un segmento en el que Jason, uno de los protagonistas, usa un arma para disparar contra un muro y escribir "Leek" con las perforaciones que dejan las balas. Esto es una referencia directa a CyberLeek, el nombre del grupo que se adjudica las filtraciones.
Hasta aquí, todo hacía pensar que los vídeos que se estaban divulgando se habían filtrado como tales. El análisis de los metadatos indicaba que se trataba de una build de 2023, lo que explicaba por qué el material se veía tan falto de pulido. Pero si los autores de los actuales leaks de GTA 6 realmente tienen una versión jugable en su poder, es un problema mayúsculo para Rockstar y su casa matriz, Take-Two Interactive.
Hoy por hoy, nadie puede descartar que próximas filtraciones de GTA 6 no sean de vídeos de gameplay, sino del juego en sí mismo. Si una versión sin terminar del nuevo Grand Theft Auto llegara a manos de los jugadores antes de tiempo, podría ser catastrófico para uno de los lanzamientos más importantes de todos los tiempos. Al menos desde un punto de vista de marketing y relaciones públicas, claro está.
Los filtradores de GTA 6 tendrían una versión jugable en su poder
Si una versión jugable de GTA 6 realmente ha escapado de los servidores de Rockstar y T2, es un gran fiasco para ambas compañías. Tanto el estudio como el publisher han apostado por el máximo secretismo posible respecto del juego, más allá de lo poco que hemos podido ver hasta aquí en los dos tráilers y las imágenes oficiales.
De hecho, las empresas se han convertido en blanco de críticas por parte del público por no ofrecer un vistazo real a la jugabilidad de GTA 6. El primer contacto real de los fans con el gameplay del nuevo Grand Theft Auto ha sido con las filtraciones de esta semana, lo que valida ese descontento.
CyberLeek sostiene que las filtraciones son a modo de protesta por la decisión de no lanzar GTA 6 en formato físico. Por supuesto que hay que tomar esa afirmación con pinzas, considerando que el grupo también se está lucrando con la promoción de una memecoin. Independientemente de la motivación real de los perpetradores, es un hecho que la campaña de promoción del título ha sido mediocre hasta el momento.
Sea como sea, el panorama no pinta bien para Rockstar y Take-Two Interactive. Ninguna de las dos empresas se ha pronunciado públicamente sobre el asunto hasta el momento. Los leaks se dan en el momento más inoportuno, considerando que la próxima semana se estrenará en Netflix un vistazo extendido a GTA 6. Una decisión que también ha provocado polémica, considerando que dicho material será exclusivo de la plataforma de streaming durante 6 horas antes de llegar a YouTube.

articles.title: AirPods with cameras could not arrive at a worse time — and I'll just say no
articles.text:
AirPods with cameras could not arrive at a worse time — and I'll just say no
There's a reason our ears don't also have eyes
Here's something I never thought: What if my ears could see? The very idea of it conjures visions of earlobes with clusters of tiny, spider-like eyes.
Of course, now we're all considering this possibility thanks to what appears to be a stunning crack in Apple's typically rock-solid dome of product secrecy.
As we reported earlier this week, MacRumors dug into one of the macOS 27 release candidates and unearthed a short bit of video featuring a man wearing AirPods Pro earbuds but somehow using them with Apple Intelligence to save an image of a book for later.
The guy isn't wearing glasses, so it's not the rumored Apple iGlass or Apple Vision Wear at work here. Instead, everyone believes this is the first confirmation that Apple is working on AirPods with cameras or "AirPods Vision," a pair of Bluetooth earbuds also equipped with vision sensors that, in concert with your connected iPhone, can use Apple Intelligence to recognize objects and then store information about them for retrieval later.
I spent some time staring at the bud in the guy's ear, and it looks, from this angle, exactly like the current AirPods Pro 3 I currently wear. I assume that whatever sensors the buds are using live on the opposite side, facing out so they can "see" what you see.
I also got caught up in the book the guy is memorizing. Could, Should, Might, Don't, is a real book by former design head for Google X, Nick Foster. In it, he dives into four mindsets of, I guess, future ideation and innovation:
- "Could" revolves around the wild possibilities (probably why we watch and love Star Trek).
- "Should" is sort of the realist's approach to what we should do based on on-the-ground facts and data.
- "Might" appears to combine elements of the first two.
- "Don't" is the risk-averse part. It's all the reasons people don't want Artificial General Intelligence or robots running AGI living with, working with, and maybe ultimately controlling us.
While not anti-tech or anti-innovation, the book has a point of view and seems an odd choice to include in what might be an iPhone and AirPods tip video.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
I look at the overall image and that book and think:
"Yeah, we Could do this, have AirPods that can see, but we Should think about the consequences of another sensor on our body, and while it Might be cool to have an always-aware system memorizing things for you, we Don't want other people to freak out when they see cameras in our ears."
Smart Glasses is a lesson
Usually, I would remind people that these are all rumors and Apple is always working on oddball stuff that will never see the light of day, but we have a tip video. Apple doesn't create tips for products it's never bringing to market.
I think there's a good chance we will get these "seeing" AirPods Pro this year. I understand the system probably isn't collecting and storing images of everything you see forever. It appears to be on demand, and the use of Apple Vision should mean that it takes the image, sends it to Apple's Private Cloud Compute, matches it with available data on the internet — "What is this book?" — and stores that data without the need for the actual photo or anything else the AirPods Pro's sensors detected.
Even with those assurances, consumers are in no mood for more wearable sensors. Just look at the growing negative sentiment around smart glasses, which some are now calling "creep glasses."
The difference, of course, is that such smart wearable cameras are meant to both analyze the world you see and to capture and store photos and videos. The "creep" factor comes in from people circumventing the onboard privacy controls (trying to hide the LED lights) so they can surreptitiously capture photos and videos.
The problem with camera- or vision-equipped AirPods, though, is that people will have similar concerns. If they see cameras on your AirPods, they will surely recoil and demand to know what they're for and if you are capturing images and video of them. You might say no, but also secretly wish you had. The chance to document at least their face and name so you don't forget it the next time you see them would be too hard to pass up.
AirPods Vision, if that's what they're called, might not allow you to capture images of living things, something that could seriously limit their utility except for use in quiet, windowsless, and people-free rooms like the one that guy is standing in. Oh, wait, that has a window. What if someone walks by? Does the AirPods' vision system stop working?
In a few weeks, Apple will have a new CEO, John Ternus, who will want to put his stamp on the company. This could be his first opportunity. I know Tim Cook loved the idea of AR glasses and was definitely all in on sensor-filled wearables, especially ones that could improve your health and safety.
Ternus could recalibrate, though. I'm sure he'll continue to support the health and safety aspect, but maybe he pumps the brakes on glasses and these AirPods with cameras until he has a better understanding of public sentiment and the privacy implications. There's a lot to discover, and given the challenges in these markets, there's no need to rush into anything.

articles.title: A fantastical journey unfolds in gorgeous Wildwood trailer
articles.text:
In June, we highlighted a behind-the-scenes featurette on the making of Wildwood, director Travis Knight’s forthcoming stop-motion animated fantasy film. Laika Studios released an extended teaser in May, which racked up over 90 million views. And now we’ve got the gorgeous full trailer, set to a haunting cover of Avicii’s “Wake Me Up.”
The film is an adaptation of the 2011 novel by Colin Meloy—frontman of indie folk-rock band The Decemberists—and his wife, illustrator Carson Ellis. Meloy and Ellis live in Portland, Oregon, near Forest Park, where they often hike the trails. In Wildwood, they transformed that local landmark into a magical hidden world filled with talking animals and lurking threats, only accessible to people of The Wood—and select Outsider “half-breeds.”
Twelve-year-old Prue McKee discovers the forest while out walking with her baby brother, Mac. A murder of crows swoops down and carries him away, and Prue discovers the Wilderness while hunting for him. Her schoolmate, Curtis Mehlberg, follows her, and both are able to enter that magical world. Fantastical adventures ensue as the pair encounter a mysterious woman, Alexandra, who has lost her son, along with coyotes, bandits, and some pretty big secrets.

articles.title: How Modern CX Tools Reduce Call Center Churn - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Call center staff churn creates massive operational headaches for managers across Australia. High turnover drains company budgets, lowers team morale, and damages key service scores.
Modern customer experience software offers practical solutions to keep agents engaged and satisfied. By removing daily friction points and simplifying daily tasks, smart tech setups turn high-stress environments into rewarding workplaces.
Reducing Daily Work Stress for Support Reps
Managing high call volumes without proper tools creates heavy workplace fatigue. Bringing in an experienced customer service consulting team helps companies identify operational bottlenecks before staff decides to quit. Expert advice allows organizations to restructure workflows and implement support systems that keep representatives comfortable throughout their shifts.
Clear operational structures reduce unexpected workload spikes for phone reps. Streamlined call routing directs incoming inquiries to appropriate specialists, preventing agent confusion. Supportive work environments help teams maintain focus and feel valued during hectic call queues.
Cutting Software Overload with Unified Dashboards
Agents often struggle when forced to toggle between multiple disconnected browser tabs during customer inquiries. A study by Deloitte highlights that 3 out of 4 survey respondents feel overwhelmed by excessive systems and information overload. Unified agent desktop interfaces consolidate client data into a single, clean workspace.
Single pane platforms allow reps to locate account details without searching separate databases. Eliminating digital clutter speeds up average handle times and keeps frontline workers focused on helping people. Smoother interface designs lower daily frustration, creating a far better working environment.
Research from Cornell University indicates that 87% of call center agents experience job-related stress during their shifts. Lowering interface confusion helps reduce workplace fatigue across all support tiers.
Shifting Service Desks into Revenue Drivers
Viewing support departments purely as expense centers limits investment in worker satisfaction and software tools. Data published by Nextiva suggests businesses ought to treat customer service as a revenue-generating function rather than a basic support expense. Equipping staff with cross-sell insights and upselling prompts gives daily duties a clear sense of purpose.
Agents who see their efforts drive financial growth feel higher job satisfaction. Performance incentives tied to successful resolutions boost confidence across the floor. Upgraded tech platforms track sales metrics in real time, celebrating team wins as they happen.
Providing staff with clear progression pathways keeps ambition high within support units. Team members feel valued when management rewards performance through transparent metrics. Purpose-driven workplaces experience significantly lower resignation rates over long periods.
Lowering Financial Costs Associated with Agent Turnover
High employee churn places a heavy financial penalty on call center operations each year. Recent industry figures from Ringly show that replacing 1 agent costs between $10,000 and $20,000 in direct recruitment and training expenses. Industry reports from The GTM Advisor note that call center agent turnover runs between 30% and 45% annually across sectors.
Smart retention strategies combined with digital upgrades protect budget margins and build experienced teams. Key operational financial benefits include:
- Reduced recruitment fees and onboarding expenses.
- Shorter ramp-up times for incoming call handlers.
- Consistent service quality for long-term customers.
- Stronger team morale and higher retention rates.
Savings generated through lower churn allow management to fund further technology upgrades. Retaining experienced representatives improves team service quality and customer retention rates.
Modernizing Cloud Systems and Automation
Legacy technology stacks force representatives to execute repetitive manual steps for every single caller. Industry insights from TTEC note that digital transformation tools, including cloud platforms, messaging, and automation, have become a complete necessity. Cloud systems deliver reliable uptime and allow teams to work securely from any location.
Flexible work arrangements help contact centers attract top talent and retain experienced phone agents. Analysis by Insignia Resource reveals remote contact centers maintain 25% to 35% lower turnover than traditional office settings. Cloud infrastructure supports remote reps with real-time assistance tools and frictionless communication channels.
Remote agent tools include cloud-based shift scheduling and instant team messaging platforms. Supervisors can offer immediate assistance during tricky calls through silent whisper modes.
Predictive Outreach to Prevent Customer Friction
Customer frustrations often spill over onto frontline staff when issues go unaddressed for long periods. Research from OnClarity demonstrates that proactive customer outreach based on predictive analytics cuts churn by 15% to 25%. Resolving account issues before customers phone in keeps queue volumes manageable.
Lower call volumes keep stress manageable for frontline service professionals. Predictive systems flag potential account risks early, letting automated workflows send status updates or solutions directly to clients. Smooth client communications create peaceful shift conditions for phone teams.
Fewer angry callers entering queues protect the mental well-being of support staff. Automated notification channels handle routine updates, so reps focus on meaningful interactions.
Call center churn does not need to remain an accepted cost of running a business. Implementing smart CX software gives frontline representatives clean interfaces, useful automation, and flexible working conditions. Companies that prioritize employee experience build loyal teams, save money, and deliver superior customer satisfaction day after day.

articles.title: L’arrivée de Siri AI sur Apple TV 4K se confirme, mais l’Europe pose problème
articles.text:
Le système d’exploitation tvOS 27 intègre dorénavant une application Siri AI. Si elle n’est pour l’instant pas fonctionnelle, cette application annonce clairement l’arrivée de l’assistant IA d’Apple sur l’Apple TV 4K. Bonne nouvelle donc pour les amateurs de produits Apple, mais un problème de taille survient : Apple AI est pour l’instant bloqué en Europe.
Siri AI intégré à tvOS 27 : son arrivée sur l’Apple TV 4K se confirme
En juin dernier, Apple a dévoilé en grande pompe Siri AI, sa nouvelle intelligence artificielle dopée par Gemini. L’entreprise à la pomme avait alors mis l’accent sur son intégration sur l’iPhone, l’iPad ou encore l’Apple Watch. En revanche, nous n’avions eu aucune information concernant son déploiement sur l’Apple TV 4K et le Home Pod. La raison est simple : Siri AI n’était pas encore totalement prêt à intégrer ces deux appareils. Apple a donc préféré attendre.
Mais les choses semblent maintenant bouger. En effet, tvOS 27 intègre désormais Siri AI dans sa liste d’applications en faisant apparaître une référence baptisée « com.apple.campo ». À l’heure actuelle, cette application n’est pas fonctionnelle et indique lorsqu’on tente de la lancer : « Refus de la demande d’ouverture de l’application : désactivée (« com.apple.campo » n’est pas activée) ».
Autant dire que ce refus de lancement est temporaire et que cette application, pour l’instant non fonctionnelle, annonce l’arrivée de Siri AI sur l’Apple TV 4K. Le nouvel assistant IA d’Apple intégrera par ailleurs le HomePod, puisque le système d’exploitation de l’enceinte repose sur une variante de tvOS, et plus généralement la nouvelle génération d’appareils Apple pour la maison connectée qui devrait être présentée cet automne.
Une arrivée attendue, mais compromise ?
En réalité, l’arrivée de Siri AI sur les appareils domotiques d’Apple est attendue. L’entreprise à la pomme devrait même en faire son principal argument de vente. Mais si l’Apple TV 4K et le HomePod devraient prendre une nouvelle dimension avec Siri AI, il reste un point central à éclaircir : leurs fonctionnalités pourront-elles être pleinement déployées en Europe ?
Pour rappel, Siri AI est bloqué en Europe. Dès lors, pour un citoyen européen, quel est l’intérêt d’acheter une Apple TV 4K s’il ne peut pas bénéficier de sa principale nouveauté, à savoir Siri AI ? Il reste à espérer que l’Union européenne et Apple trouvent un terrain d’entente d’ici la commercialisation en Europe de la nouvelle gamme domotique d’Apple.

articles.title: Des vidéos montrent le lanceur Zhuque-3 de LandSpace vaciller juste après l'atterrissage
articles.text:
L’espace est difficile, mais le retour sur Terre n’est pas non plus une partie de plaisir. On peut le deviner avec l’historique récent de la société chinoise LandSpace. Il y a huit mois, sa fusée Zhuque-3 s’écrasait lourdement lors de sa tentative d’atterrissage — une scène capturée en haute définition. C’était le tout premier essai du groupe.
Le nouveau test organisé fin août s’est clairement mieux passé, puisque le nouvel exemplaire du lanceur Zhuque-3 a pu se poser comme une Falcon 9. De là à dire que tout a été parfait pour LandSpace ? Pas sûr : des vidéos supplémentaires partagées sur les réseaux sociaux ont montré que le premier étage ZQ-3 a eu des bouffées de chaleur qui auraient pu mal tourner.
Ainsi, juste après s’être posé avec délicatesse dans le désert de Gobi (nord de la Chine), le lanceur devait être sécurisé. Dans la foulée du vol, il y a donc eu un déploiement de petits robots pompiers téléguidés pour asperger la base de l’engin, là où se trouvent les moteurs, afin d’éteindre les flammes résiduelles autour des tuyères.
Mais ce travail semble avoir été plus difficile qu’escompté. Comme l’a relevé le compte spécialisé dans l’actualité spatiale chinoise @CNSpaceflight sur X (ex-Twitter), « il semble que l’extinction de l’incendie ne se soit pas déroulée comme prévu ». C’est ce que montre une capture d’écran d’une vidéo, avec une importante gerbe de flammes jaillissant de la base.
La séquence suggère ainsi un feu important, avec des flammes léchant une partie du cylindre ainsi que ses pieds. Une importante fumée noire est aussi visible, tandis que dans un coin de la capture, on peut apercevoir l’arrivée des robots pompiers sur la zone d’atterrissage. Sur d’autres vidéos, on les voyait à l’œuvre, mais sans voir l’étendue du feu.
Une fusée qui tangue un peu
La présence de ce brasier a pu causer un effet mécanique sur la structure : un affaiblissement d’un des pieds. C’est en tout cas ce que l’on peut déduire d’une autre scène proposée en accéléré — et également partagée sur X par le compte @CNSpaceflight. On voit en effet la fusée légèrement vaciller sur un côté, comme si un pied était en souffrance.
On peut supposer que c’est sous l’effet de la chaleur intense et prolongée que cette jambe d’atterrissage a été fragilisée, et qu’il ne s’agit pas d’un tangage causé par le vent de Gobi. La vidéo donne en tout cas matière à penser que le pied sur lequel le poids du lanceur repose davantage est un peu plus tordu que les autres.
@CNSpaceflight avance que cette inclinaison est « probablement due à l’affaiblissement d’une jambe causé par l’incendie ». Cependant, à ce stade de ce que l’on sait, le désastre matériel a, semble-t-il, été évité. Certes, l’engin donne l’impression qu’il pourrait basculer et s’écraser au sol d’une seconde à l’autre, mais sans que cela ne survienne vraiment.
« Il n’y a aucune preuve que le propulseur soit tombé », ajoute le compte @CNSpaceflight malgré une posture inquiétante pour un lanceur de cette taille — s’il avait trop penché de biais, il aurait sans doute fini par basculer et s’écraser sur l’aire d’atterrissage de tout son long. Dans le récapitulatif officiel de LandSpace en tout cas, ce n’est pas un sujet.
